title: Esterification as a reversible reaction
keyIdea: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react, with an acid catalyst, to give an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. Water can hydrolyse the ester back, so the reaction is reversible and reaches dynamic equilibrium. For ethanoic acid and ethanol Kc = [ester][water]/([acid][alcohol]) ≈ 4, so starting from 1 mol of each, only about 0.67 mol of ester forms. To raise the yield, use an excess of the cheaper reactant (usually the alcohol) or remove a product as it forms (take out the water, or distil off the low-boiling ester). The catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it shortens the time to equilibrium but does not change Kc or the yield, and because ΔH is close to zero, heating mainly changes the rate too.
familyTip: Ask: if you mix 1 mol of acid with 1 mol of ethanol and wait as long as you like, how much ester do you get? Most people say 1 mol. Then work it out together from Kc = 4: x²/(1 − x)² = 4, so x/(1 − x) = 2 and x = 2/3. Ask what changes when you add a second mole of ethanol, and why the answer is not double.

visual.caption: What does each change do to the equilibrium yield of ester? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build the equation, add excess ethanol, remove water or ester, race catalyst and heat, sort changes.

kid: An acid and an alcohol can join to make an ester and water. This is esterification. Ethanoic acid and ethanol make ethyl ethanoate. It is the sweet smell in some nail varnish remover. A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid are the catalyst.

The reaction can run both ways. Water can split the ester back into acid and alcohol. This is hydrolysis. In a closed flask both reactions run at the same rate in the end. That is dynamic equilibrium. Here Kc is about 4. So 1 mol of each only gives about 0.67 mol of ester.

You can push it to the right. Add more of one reactant, often the cheaper alcohol. With 3 mol of ethanol per mole of acid, about 90% of the acid turns into ester. Or take a product away as it forms. Dry out the water, or boil off the ester. It has the lowest boiling point in the flask.

The catalyst speeds up both ways by the same amount. You reach equilibrium in an hour, not months. But the yield stays the same. Heat does much the same here. ΔH is close to zero, so Kc hardly changes when it gets hot.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This is A-level chemistry: esters (AQA 3.3.9, OCR A 6.1.3) with chemical equilibria and Kc. It links to NGSS HS-PS1-6, which asks students to change conditions to get more product at equilibrium. Students write the equation and Kc. They explain the role of the catalyst. They suggest and justify ways to raise the yield.

There are two moles on each side, so the volume cancels in Kc. You can use moles directly. Kc is about 4 at room temperature. From a 1 : 1 start, x²/(1 − x)² = 4 gives x = 2/3. Berthelot and Péan de Saint-Gilles found this limit in 1862. With b mol of ethanol per mole of acid, x² = 4(1 − x)(b − x). Then b = 2 gives 0.85 and b = 3 gives 0.90, so returns shrink. Removing water, or boiling off the ester at 77 °C, lowers a product. Qc drops below Kc, and the forward reaction catches up.

Common mistakes. Students write a one-way arrow, or say it goes to completion. They write Kc upside down, or leave out water. Water is a product in the same liquid, so it stays in. They say the catalyst raises the yield or Kc. They say excess alcohol raises Kc, when it only moves the position. They mix up acid hydrolysis, which is reversible, with alkaline hydrolysis. That one goes to completion, as the carboxylate ion cannot react with the alcohol. One nuance: a lot of concentrated sulfuric acid also soaks up water. That is a water-removal effect, not a catalyst effect.

In the lab the learner builds the equation from six cards. They reject ethene and put the catalyst over the arrow. They drag the ethanol from 1 to 5 mol to hit 80%, 90% and 94%. They remove water or boil off ester until over 90% of the acid is used. They run four catalyst and heat settings and see 0.67 mol each time. Last, they sort seven changes into more ester, less ester or no change.

practice.hint: Is the reaction reversible, and what small molecule is lost?
practice.explain: Water is the second product and it can hydrolyse the ester back, so the reaction is written with ⇌.

practice.prompt: At equilibrium [acid] = [ethanol] = 0.5 mol dm⁻³, [ester] = {e} mol dm⁻³ and [water] = {w} mol dm⁻³. Work out Kc.
practice.explain: Kc = ({e} × {w}) / (0.5 × 0.5) = {e} × {w} × 4 = {=4*e*w}. There are no units, as two moles sit on each side.

practice.prompt: Which change does not alter the equilibrium yield of ester?
practice.hint: Which one speeds up both directions equally?
practice.explain: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and back reactions alike, so Kc and the yield are unchanged.

practice.prompt: Start with {=3*n} mol of ethanoic acid and {=3*n} mol of ethanol. Kc = 4. How many moles of ester are there at equilibrium?
practice.explain: x = 2({=3*n} − x), so 3x = {=6*n} and x = {=2*n} mol. Two thirds of the acid becomes ester.

practice.prompt: Why does heating an ester with NaOH(aq) go to completion when acid hydrolysis does not?
choices: The carboxylic acid becomes a carboxylate ion that cannot re-form the ester
NaOH is a catalyst that removes the back reaction
The reaction with NaOH is strongly endothermic
practice.hint: What does the base do to the acid as it forms?
practice.explain: OH⁻ deprotonates the acid to RCOO⁻. The ion does not react with the alcohol, so the back reaction is removed.

pool.prompt: What is the Kc expression for ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water?
pool.hint: Products on top; every species in the liquid mixture appears.
pool.explain: Products over reactants. Water is a product in the same phase, so it is included.

pool.prompt: Why is excess ethanol usually used rather than excess ethanoic acid?
choices: Ethanol is cheaper and easy to remove, and either excess moves the position right
Excess acid stops the catalyst working
pool.hint: Both are reactants. What decides which one to use in excess?
pool.explain: An excess of either reactant moves the position right. The cheaper, easily separated one is chosen, often the alcohol.

pool.prompt: Adding a catalyst to the equilibrium mixture will…
choices: leave the amount of ester unchanged
pool.hint: A catalyst speeds both directions by the same factor.
pool.explain: At equilibrium the catalyst changes nothing: forward and back rates rise equally, so the position and Kc stay the same.

pool.prompt: Kc = 4. At equilibrium [acid] = {u} mol dm⁻³, [alcohol] = {v} mol dm⁻³ and [water] = 2 mol dm⁻³. What is [ester] in mol dm⁻³?
Ethyl ethanoate is distilled off as it forms. What happens to the equilibrium?
choices: It moves right and more ester forms
It moves left and more acid forms
pool.hint: A product is being removed. How does the system respond?
pool.explain: Removing the ester lowers Qc below Kc, so the forward reaction outruns the back one until Qc = Kc again.

pool.prompt: The enthalpy change for esterification is close to zero. What does raising the temperature mainly do?
choices: Reach equilibrium faster with almost the same yield
pool.hint: How does Kc depend on temperature when ΔH ≈ 0?
pool.explain: With ΔH close to zero Kc barely changes with temperature, so heating mainly increases the rate.

pool.prompt: Start with {=3*n} mol of acid and {=3*n} mol of ethanol. Kc = 4. How many moles of acid are left at equilibrium?
pool.hint: Two thirds of the acid turns into ester when the start is 1 : 1.
pool.explain: x = 2/3 × {=3*n} = {=2*n} mol of ester, so {=3*n} − {=2*n} = {=n} mol of acid is left.

pool.prompt: Which statement about dynamic equilibrium in esterification is correct?
choices: Ester still forms and hydrolyses, at equal rates
Only the forward reaction is still running
pool.explain: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions keep going at the same rate, so the amounts stay constant.

pool.prompt: Which is the best way to increase the yield of ester from a 1 : 1 mixture?
choices: Remove the water as it forms
Add more concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst only
pool.hint: Which change lowers a product concentration?
pool.explain: Removing water lowers [H₂O], so Qc < Kc and the position moves right. Adding water does the opposite.
